title: Rock clouds that vanish: JWST reveals extreme weather on distant exoplanet
summary:
For two decades, exoplanet scientists have been frustrated by clouds. On Hot Jupiters—gas giants that orbit perilously close to their stars—thick, pervasive cloud decks have acted like a foggy window, obscuring the atmospheres beneath. But now, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has finally cut through the haze. In a study published in Science, researchers report the first direct observation of a dramatic daily cloud cycle on WASP-94A b, a planet 700 light-years away.

The team, led by Sagnick Mukherjee and David Sing of Johns Hopkins University, used JWST to observe the planet as it transited its star. By separately analyzing the light from the leading edge (morning) and trailing edge (evening), they uncovered a stark dichotomy. The morning side was thick with clouds of magnesium silicate—literally, rock vapor condensed into tiny particles. The evening side, however, was nearly cloud-free. "It was a huge surprise," Sing said. "People have expected some differences, like it's cooler in the morning than the evening... But what we saw was a real dichotomy."

What causes this vanishing act? Two theories: either powerful atmospheric winds drag the clouds deep into the planet's scorching day side, hiding them from view, or the clouds simply evaporate as temperatures soar past 1,000°C. The latter is like morning fog burning off on Earth, but under conditions more extreme than any terrestrial weather. This cycle not only reveals the planet's dynamic climate but also gave scientists a pristine view of its atmosphere. Previous observations with the Hubble Space Telescope had averaged the cloudy and clear regions together, leading to misleading estimates—suggesting the planet had hundreds of times more oxygen and carbon than Jupiter. The new data corrects that: WASP-94A b has only about five times more, aligning with planet formation theories.

The breakthrough demonstrates JWST's power to localize observations, effectively clearing the fog. The team has already spotted similar cloud cycling on two other Hot Jupiters, WASP-39 b and WASP-17 b, and plans a larger survey. Understanding these alien weather patterns not only satisfies curiosity but also helps refine models of atmospheric chemistry under extreme irradiation—a key step in characterizing potentially habitable worlds.
why_it_matters: The ability to resolve weather patterns on a planet 700 light-years away shows how far technology has come and brings us closer to understanding the climates of Earth-like worlds, which could one day help identify habitable exoplanets.

background_read: When the first exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star was discovered in 1995, it was a 'Hot Jupiter' — a gas giant far closer to its star than Mercury is to the Sun. These worlds were a shock, and studying their atmospheres has been difficult because thick clouds often block the view. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST, launched in 2021 as the most powerful space observatory ever built), with its infrared sensitivity, can peer through some hazes and, crucially, separate the light from different parts of the planet as it crosses its star. Earlier, the Hubble Space Telescope (a smaller, 1990-era telescope) could only average the whole atmosphere, leading to blended signals. WASP-94A b, 700 light-years away, now provides the first full picture of a daily rock-vapor cloud cycle — a dramatic example of alien weather.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Thick clouds on Hot Jupiters have hidden atmospheres for two decades.
KEY DISCOVERY: JWST captures first daily cloud cycle on exoplanet WASP-94A b.
├─ TEAM: Sagnick Mukherjee & David Sing (Johns Hopkins)
└─ METHOD: Analyzing light from morning (leading) and evening (trailing) edges during transit.
├─ MORNING: Dense magnesium silicate clouds – like rock vapor dust.
├─ WIND: Powerful winds drag clouds to the scorching day side.
└─ EVAPORATION: Clouds burn off like morning fog at >1,000°C.
├─ HUBBLE AVERAGING: Suggested oxygen & carbon 100s of times Jupiter's level.
└─ JWST LOCALIZED: Only ~5 times more, fitting planet formation models.
FUTURE: Similar cycling seen on WASP-39 b and WASP-17 b, larger survey planned to study alien weather.

perspectives.description: JWST's vision ends decades of atmospheric frustration, revealing alien weather in remarkable detail. This breakthrough will improve models of planet formation and could be a stepping stone to detecting biosignatures on rocky worlds.

The planet studied is an uninhabitable gas giant with temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock; these extreme conditions don't directly inform about Earth-like worlds. Moreover, interpreting cloud behavior from subtle light curves still carries uncertainties.

The discovery fits a pattern: Hot Jupiters likely have dynamic cloud cycles driven by intense stellar radiation and strong winds. Localized observations, rather than disk-averaged data, are essential — much like weather satellites gave us a global view of Earth's weather.

Having spotted cloud cycling on three Hot Jupiters, astronomers plan larger surveys to build a database that could reveal common climate rules. Future telescopes designed for habitable-zone planets will benefit from these techniques, making the search for life more precise.
